statements.text: design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems and physical systems

understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking [for example, ones for sorting and searching]; use logical reasoning to compare the utility of alternative algorithms for the same problem

use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems; make appropriate use of data structures [for example, lists, tables or arrays]; design and develop modular programs that use procedures or functions

understand simple Boolean logic [for example, AND, OR and NOT] and some of its uses in circuits and programming; understand how numbers can be represented in binary, and be able to carry out simple operations on binary numbers [for example, binary addition, and conversion between binary and decimal]
understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems

statements.short: How computers store instructions and data
statements.text: understand how instructions are stored and executed within a computer system; understand how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally, in the form of binary digits

undertake creative projects that involve selecting, using, and combining multiple applications, preferably across a range of devices, to achieve challenging goals, including collecting and analysing data and meeting the needs of known users
create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability

understand a range of ways to use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, including protecting their online identity and privacy; recognise inappropriate content, contact and conduct, and know how to report concerns

units.title: Problem Solving and Design
units.subtitle: Computational thinking and algorithm design
units.summary: Students learn to think like problem solvers: breaking problems down, spotting patterns and writing instructions so clear that a robot can follow them. Everything is unplugged, so no computers or software are needed.
lessons: Think Like Problem Solvers: decomposition and pattern recognition
Algorithm Design: Write It Clearly and Program the Robot
Robot Delivery Mission: plan, write, test and debug a robot program
Revision and End of Unit Test (35 marks), then feedback

abstraction: Robot grids and a school map model real places as squares, and a trace table records the robot's position and direction after each line. Abstraction is named and taught as a skill in Year 8.
algorithms: Students compare clear and unclear instructions, shorten a program with MOVE FORWARD (number), and use logical reasoning to find the line with the bug. Sorting and searching come in later units.
programming: Exact robot commands in sequence, and data in tables (a Sports Day timetable and trace tables). No programming language is used in this unit.

units.title: Problem Solving and Design
units.subtitle: Computational thinking and algorithm design
units.summary: Students use all four computational thinking skills, then design algorithms three ways: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode, with decisions and loops. The unit ends with Robo's Rescue Mission, a three-lesson design project.
lessons: Pseudocode: Decisions and loops (IF … ELSE, WHILE)
Robo's Rescue Mission: plan, build, test, debug and share
Revision, End of Unit Test (45 marks) and a feedback lesson

abstraction: A busy picture becomes a grid model; robot grids model rooms, walls, doors and keys in every algorithm lesson; trace tables record the robot's state after each step.
algorithms: Students compare 16 separate steps with a REPEAT loop, and a WHILE loop with a fixed distance, then find and fix errors in flowcharts and pseudocode. Sorting and searching come in later units.
programming: Sequence, selection (IF … ELSE) and iteration (REPEAT, WHILE) in pseudocode with exact keywords and indentation: the foundations for a textual language. No programming language is used in this unit.

units.title: Problem Solving and Design
units.subtitle: Algorithms in pseudocode
units.summary: Students move from robot commands to the pseudocode used in Cambridge IGCSE, starting with variables, input and output. The first lesson is ready, and more lessons are on the way.
lessons: Pseudocode 1: Robo Learns to Listen (variables, INPUT and OUTPUT)

programming: Variables as named stores of data, and INPUT and OUTPUT in pseudocode, in the style used by Cambridge IGCSE.
